guideRowNote: A full explanation of karuta and its rules!
guideIntro: Karuta looks wild and fast, but the rules are simple. Here's the whole game in a few minutes.
guidePoems1: Hyakunin Isshu means “one poem each from a hundred poets”. About 800 years ago the poet Fujiwara no Teika chose 100 short poems, each by a different person.
guidePoems2: Every poem has 31 sounds in five parts of 5, 7, 5, 7 and 7. The first three parts are the first half. The last two are the second half.
guidePoems3: Many families play with these cards at New Year. Competitive karuta is the sport version. Two players kneel face to face and race to take the right card first.
guideCardsTitle: The reader and two kinds of cards
guideCards1: Every match has a reader. The reader doesn't play. They read the poems out loud, one at a time, in a random order.
guideCards2: There are two sets of 100 cards. A reading card (yomifuda) has the whole poem, and only the reader uses it. A taking card (torifuda) shows just the second half, written in hiragana. These are the cards on the floor.
guideCardsTobi: So you hear how a poem starts and grab the card with how it ends!
guideStep1: The 100 taking cards are mixed face down. Each player gets 25. The other 50 are left out.
guideStep2: You lay your 25 cards in three rows in front of you. That's your side. The other player's side is right across from it.
guideStep3: Then you have 15 minutes to remember where every card is, on both sides.
guideStep4: The reader starts with a warm-up poem that isn't one of the 100. Then the real cards begin.
guideStep5: When a poem is read, touch its card before the other player does. It can be on either side. Sweeping it off the field with your hand counts too.
guideStep6: If you take a card from their side, you send one of your own cards over to them.
guideStep7: The first player to clear their own side wins.
guideMatchTobi: Fifteen minutes only to remember? Yep. Good players know where all 50 cards are.
guideFault1: Remember the 50 cards that were left out? The reader reads those too. They're called dead cards. If a dead card is read and you touch a card on the field, that's a fault.
guideFault2: Touching the wrong side is a fault as well. If the card read is on your side and you touch one on their side, it's a fault, and the same the other way round. Touching another card on the right side is fine.
guideFault3: After a fault, the other player sends you one of their cards. So you need to be quick, but also to wait for the right moment.
guideFaultTobi: Oops! I went for a dead card again.
guideKimariji1: Here's the big secret. You don't have to hear the whole poem. Its first few sounds tell you which card it is. Those sounds are called its kimariji, the deciding sounds.
guideOne: Seven poems start with a sound no other poem starts with. Hear that one sound and you can go. Players remember them as {0}.
guideLong: Most poems share their first sounds with another poem. {0} and {1} both start with {2}, so {2} isn't enough. You have to wait for the third sound.
guideLongCaption: The red sound decides. Both are 3-sound cards.
guideChange: Each card is read only once. After {0} has been read, {1} is the only card left that starts with {2}. Now {2} is enough, so it has become a 2-sound card.
guideChangeCaption: One is gone, so two sounds are enough now.
guideSix: The longest kimariji have six sounds. {0}, {1} and {2} each start two poems, and only the sixth sound tells them apart.
guideKimarijiTobi: Kimariji are the heart of karuta. Know them well and your hand moves before the poem ends!
guideApp1: This app trains the part that matters most. A card appears, you say its kimariji and swipe it away as fast as you can. Every swipe is timed.
guideApp2: On the journey, new cards come in a few at a time, and cards you're about to forget come back at the right moment. Once you know all 100, take the graduation exam. Pass it and ranked mode opens, where your speed sets your rank.
guideAppTobi: I'll be with you the whole way. See you in Training!

rulesSource: These are the official competition rules of the All Japan Karuta Association (一般社団法人全日本かるた協会), called 競技規程細則. They came into force in September 2008 and were last updated on 26 May 2020.
rulesDisclaimer: The English version is a translation made by this app. Only the Japanese version is the actual rules.
rulesDisclaimerShort: Translation by this app. Only the Japanese text is the actual rules.

aboutLadderLead: Each step down is a shorter sound. It is enough once the other cards on that step have been read.
aboutLadderLeadKana: Whole kana only. Each step down is one kana shorter.
ladderTop: Only this card starts like this, so this is always enough.
ladderStep: {0} cards start with {1}. Enough once the other {2} are gone:
ladderStepOne: {0} cards start with {1}. Enough once the other one is gone:
ladderConsonantStep: {0} cards start with {1}. Enough on the consonant once the other {2} are gone:

aboutMyRecordNote: Speed, attempts and memory, on the Stats page
firstSoundsIntro: Every card's About page has stairs made of sounds. They show how much of a poem you need to hear. Let's walk down them together!
firstSoundsKimariji1: The reader reads each poem from its first sound. You don't have to wait for the rest. As soon as you know which card it is, you can take it.
firstSoundsKimariji2: The first sounds that tell you are the card's kimariji. They are enough because no other card starts that way.
firstSoundsKimariji3: Card {0} starts with {1} and card {2} with {3}. Both start with {4}, so {4} is not enough. The next sound tells them apart. That's why the kimariji of card {0} is {1}.
firstSoundsShorterTitle: Shorter as the match goes on
firstSoundsShorter1: Each card is read only once. After that it's out of play. So once card {0} ({1}) has been read, card {2} is the only card left that starts with {3}. Now {3} is enough.
firstSoundsShorterCaption: One card is gone, so fewer sounds are enough.
firstSoundsShorter2: It goes on like this. {0} cards start with {1}. Once the other {2} have all been read, the single sound {1} is enough.
firstSoundsShorter3: The stairs on a card's About page show this step by step. The top step is what you need at the start of a match. Each step down is a shorter sound. It is enough once the other cards on that step have been read.
firstSoundsShorterTobi: So remember which cards have been read. The more are gone, the less you need to hear!
firstSoundsStairs1: Here are the stairs of card {0}.
firstSoundsStairs2: The {0} line above the stairs shows the card's whole kimariji. The stairs start from there.
firstSoundsSound: The big sound is how much you need to hear on that step.
firstSoundsBadge: The badge counts the cards that start with that sound, this card included. Yellow means the sound is enough right now, because only this card starts that way. That's always the top step. Black marks a consonant step, which the next chapter explains. The other steps are white.
firstSoundsLine: The line under the sound says how many cards start that way and how many of the others have to be read first.
firstSoundsChips: The chips are the cards that join on that step. They and the cards on the steps above must all be read before the sound is enough. A chip shows a card's kimariji and number. Tap one to open that card. If there are many, tap the last chip to see the rest.
firstSoundsStairsExample: Look at the step {0}. Its badge says {1}, because {1} cards start with {0}. Its chip is card {2}, {3}. Once card {2} has been read, {0} is enough for card {4}.
firstSoundsConsonant1: A sound like ka (か) is really two sounds, a k and then an a. The k reaches you first. If no other card left has that consonant there, you can go before the vowel.
firstSoundsConsonant2: A consonant step ends in a dash, with the consonant in romaji. {0} means {1} followed by the consonant {2}.
firstSoundsConsonant3: That's why card {0}'s top step is {1}. Card {2} has {3} there, not {4}.
firstSoundsConsonant4: Card {0}'s top step is {1}. The only other card that starts with {2} is card {3} ({4}), and it goes on with a vowel. So as soon as you hear the {5}, it can only be card {0}.
firstSoundsConsonant5: Below it, {0} works the same way. Once card {1} has been read, {0} is enough.
firstSoundsConsonant6: Sounds are counted as you hear them, not as they are written. The sounds sh, ch, ts, f and j each count as one. So card {0}'s top step is {1}. Cards like {2} have s there, and s is not sh.
firstSoundsConsonantTobi: Going on the consonant takes practice. Start with the cards you know best!
firstSoundsSwitch1: The switch above the stairs picks how they are drawn. {0}, the one you start with, shows every step, consonant steps too.
firstSoundsSwitch2: {0} shows whole kana only, if you prefer to think in kana. The stairs start from the kimariji, and each step down is shorter by whole kana. The part you no longer need is drawn faded.
firstSoundsSwitch4: Your choice is kept for every card.
firstSoundsTobi: Try it in a match! Keep track of the cards that have been read, and walk down the stairs in your head.
statsAboutCardNote: The poem, both cards and its first sounds
matchTimerNote: A countdown for a match, with a warning at 2 minutes.
timerNoticeText: Counting down. Sounds at {0} minutes left and at the end.
timerNotifyTitle: Show the timer in a notification
timerNotifyReason: While the timer runs, it can show the time left in a notification, so you can check it on the lock screen or from another app. Android will ask you next.
reminderOfferBody: Spaced repetition only works if you keep coming back. Would you like me to send you a reminder tomorrow so you don't forget?
reminderOfferNote: You can turn reminders off any time in Settings.
reminderBlockedBody: Fudatobashi isn't allowed to send you notifications, so reminders stay off. To get them, allow notifications for Fudatobashi in your phone's settings, then turn on reminders in Settings › Learning.
remindersSettingNote: Tobi-kun will send you a reminder each day at midday.
remindersBlockedWarning: Notification permissions are not granted. You will not receive notifications.
reminderNoticeBody: Tobi is waiting with your daily cards!
reminderChannelNote: A reminder each day at midday to train your cards.
reviewPractiseNote: Missed and slowest. Practice runs never change your rank.
reviewPointsMade: {0} card points + {1} for being ready early
